props.title: The Wind Will Carry Us
props.initialSlug: A city filmmaker learns life's pace in rural Iran

sections.content: The Wind Will Carry Us represents Iranian master Abbas Kiarostami at his most contemplative and formally innovative. Like his earlier Taste of Cherry (1997), the film follows a city dweller's journey into rural Iran, but here Kiarostami pushes his minimalist style to new heights. The protagonist, a filmmaker pretending to be an engineer, waits in a Kurdish village to document a mourning ritual that may never come. The genius lies in what Kiarostami doesn't show - many key characters remain off-screen, their voices drifting up from unseen spaces, challenging conventional cinematic storytelling.

sections.content: The film's deliberate pacing and structural repetitions echo throughout contemporary slow cinema. You can trace its influence in Once Upon a Time in Anatolia (2011) and Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (2010) - works that similarly use landscape as a character and treat time as malleable. Kiarostami's signature car sequences, where characters traverse winding roads while engaging in philosophical dialogue, became a template for filmmakers like Nuri Bilge Ceylan and Jafar Panahi.

The film's exploration of modernity versus tradition resonates with other Iranian New Wave classics like Mohsen Makhmalbaf's Gabbeh (1996) and Samira Makhmalbaf's The Apple (1998). The protagonist's cell phone conversations - requiring him to drive to high ground for reception - create a recurring motif that perfectly captures the collision between urban technology and rural life. This theme would later be explored differently in Asghar Farhadi's About Elly (2009). SUBHEAD: Visual Poetry and Philosophical Inquiry

sections.content: Kiarostami's use of landscape photography reaches its apex here. Long shots of rolling hills and winding paths echo similar compositions in his earlier Life and Nothing More (1992), but now they're imbued with even greater metaphysical weight. The director's trademark blend of fiction and reality creates moments of transcendent beauty, particularly in scenes where the protagonist interacts with a ditch-digger he can hear but never see - a device that would influence later works like Goodbye to Language (2014) by Jean-Luc Godard.
